paper_title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Modern ML workloads run across an increasingly diverse range of hardware, from CPUs to GPUs with different architectures and capabilities (Reddi et al., 2020). As these platforms continue to evolve, the optimization strategies needed to use them efficiently evolve as well. Meanwhile, AI coding agents are increasingly being used to optimize performance-critical code. For example, frontier labs such as OpenAI report using AI models to autonomously rewrite and optimize production GPU kernels (Ferrari et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025). As AI agents take on more performancecritical optimization, an important question is whether they can adapt their optimization strategies as the underlying hardware evolves over time. In CPUs, hardware evolution often takes the form of new architectural extensions, which introduce new instructions and expose them to programmers through new interface. Extensions can improve performance, but exploiting them often requires fundamentally restructuring kernels implementation. For example, Arms matrix extensions support accumulating products directly into 2D matrix tiles, enabling implementations of matrix multiplication that differ from those based on earlier 1D vector instructions (Arm, 2026; Remke & Breuer, 2024). (Right) To study this adaptation, KERNELSHIFT constructs benchmark tasks from real-world sources and model executions using an agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline. but suboptimal code if it relies on older vector instructions when newer matrix instructions would be advantageous. To study kernel optimization under evolving hardware, we introduce KERNELSHIFT (Figure 1 (left)), benchmarking pipeline and set of environments for evaluating AI coding agents across evolving CPU architectures. The key idea is to evaluate how agents optimize matched kernels, where coverage permits, across successive architectural extensions that shift the space of performant implementations. Specifically, we evaluate agents across Arms vector and matrix extensions (i.e., Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), which provide instructions for parallelizing computations common in machine learning workloads (Stephens et al., 2017; Arm, 2026). Our work builds on growing literature on hardware-aware kernel optimization (He et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2025; Zang et al., 2026), with specific focus on sequences of hardware changes that expose progressively newer programming interfaces. We design an agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline with source-specific adapters for transforming code repositories into benchmark instances (Figure 1 (right)), together with environments that let agents iteratively optimize code using compilation and performance feedback from the target hardware (Figure 2). Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernel specifications from real-world, actively developed repositories, including workloads derived from real model executions. The pipeline and environments are designed to incorporate new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate coding agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer Arm architectural extensions. We measure both optimization performance and their use of newly available instructions, comparing their implementations against compiler-optimized code, production-library implementations, and expert kernels where available. Agents readily find headroom on established vector extensions: on SVE, they beat the auto-vectorized compiler in every source family and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74 over its Neon kernels within 40 tool calls), but fall behind Arms hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70). However, this does not reliably carry over to newer programming models: on SME2, agents end up far slower than the expert kernels. Our main contributions are: KERNELSHIFT, benchmarking pipeline and set of environments to evaluate coding agents on evolving hardware and programming interfaces. The agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline supports adding kernels and hardware configurations as software libraries and processors evolve. benchmark of 99 real-world CPU kernels built with this pipeline, including workloads derived from real model executions. An empirical study of coding agents across Arm architecture extensions, measuring both optimization performance and agents ability to exploit newly available hardware instructions.

We introduce our problem setting, motivate our use of architectural extensions to distinguish stages of CPU hardware evolution, and describe our automated pipeline for collecting benchmark instances. Specifically, we primarily focus on changes to the available instruction set through new extensions, since new extensions can introduce different ways to optimize computations and hence cause large shifts in the space of performant programs. For example, as illustrated in Figure 1, Arms Neon extension exposes fixed-width vector operations, while the later scalable vector extensions (SVE, SVE2) support code that adapts to different vector widths and provide additional vector operations. Motivated by these architectural shifts, we evaluate agents kernel optimization performance across such evolving extensions. In particular, we investigate whether the choice of extension impacts agent performance, and whether agents can effectively leverage newer intrinsics that are underrepresented in their training data. Therefore, we construct an automated benchmark framework that seamlessly accommodates new extensions as they arise. The benchmark design and automated generation techniques are detailed next.

Human input is limited to few decisions: selecting kernels, approving workloads where no model execution can be traced, and reviewing the resulting expert references. Appendix documents the complete construction process. Kernel and reference construction. For each source repository, construction agent follows fixed procedure (Appendix B.1) to identify candidate kernel computations and extract their fixed configuration parameters and variable workload dimensions. It then constructs portable C++ starting implementation using simple loop-based code. When the repository contains an optimized implementation of the same kernel, the agent also extracts it as the optimized reference. Workload construction. To capture realistic workloads, we derive input configurations from real model executions whenever possible. For model-derived kernels, the construction agent first identifies the source model in which the kernel appears. Fixed configuration parameters then come from this model, while dimensions are collected from execution traces. For example, ncnn workloads come from vision-model executions, while llama.cpp workloads are collected during LLM inference on ShareGPT prompts (ShareGPT, 2023). We keep the observed tensor shapes rather than the original activation values, under the assumption that kernel performance is driven primarily by tensor dimensions and operator configuration rather than the specific numerical values of the activations. We then deduplicate and subsample the collected shapes to form the hidden evaluation workloads. For kernels without clearly identifiable source model, we instead synthesize workloads in two groups: correctness-oriented cases that cover corner cases, and performance-oriented cases that probe efficiency over representative problem sizes. More details appear in Appendix B.2. Finalizing benchmark tasks. Finally, we package the starting implementation, agent-visible context, evaluation workloads, and the optimized reference from the source library, when available, into self-contained benchmark task. Each task is validated by compiling and running the starting implementation on the target hardware before it is included in KERNELSHIFT.

sections.title: 2.2 BENCHMARK COMPOSITION AND COVERAGE
sections.content: We apply the construction framework from Section 2.1 to several widely used, performance-critical open-source repositories. Composition. KERNELSHIFT currently contains kernel tasks derived from four sources  (Table 1)  : ncnn (Tencent, 2017), llama.cpp (Gerganov & ggml-org contributors, 2023), Arm SIMD Loops (Arm, 2025), and KleidiAI (Arm, 2024). Together, they cover computer-vision and LLM inference kernels, general SIMD workloads, and vendor-optimized microkernels across range of data types and optimization patterns. The ncnn and llama.cpp tasks are derived from 11 source models, providing kernel configurations representative of real model architectures. Appendices and A.2 provide the full composition and per-generation coverage. Workloads. KERNELSHIFT contains approximately 1.6K workloads across the 99 kernel specifications, constructed as described in Section 2.1 and spanning broad range of tensor dimensions and sequence lengths. sections.title: 2.3 EVALUATION ENVIRONMENT
sections.content: KERNELSHIFT uses centralized control plane to run agent harnesses and coordinate evaluation across distributed target machines (Figure 2). Hardware-in-the-loop evaluation. Each target platform is backed by an evaluator running directly on its hardware. When an agent calls tool, the request is routed to this evaluator, which compiles and executes the candidate on the target machine and returns the feedback, so that correctness and performance measurements reflect the hardware being evaluated. This design decouples the agent harness from target-specific execution, allowing the same agent setup to be used across hardware platforms. Appendix gives the deployment configurations. Unified agent interface. To compare different agent systems under the same environment, KERNELSHIFT exposes harness-agnostic interface through which all agents access the benchmark. The interface provides the same three benchmark tools to every harness: compile, evaluate, and disassemble. These tools allow agents to iteratively refine their solutions with correctness, performance, and low-level instruction feedback from the target hardware. Appendix C.3 provides the complete prompts, skills, and tool schemas. Measurement and integrity. Correctness is checked before performance is measured, and both agent implementations and comparison baselines are tested on the same target machine under the same timing protocol. We use wall-clock execution time as the common performance measure across platforms, since hardware cycle counters are not consistently available on all target systems. Performance is reported as the speedup of kernel over its expert reference on the same machine. Measurements use repeated runs on single core, and each evaluation runs in an isolated process to prevent interference between evaluations. We also reject implementations that violate the benchmark constraints, such as using multithreading. Full timing, isolation, and integrity details are provided in Appendix C.4.

sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Models and harnesses. We evaluate six frontier language models: Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic, 2026b) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026c), GPT-5.6-sol and GPT-5.6-luna (Ferrari et al., 2026), DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and GLM-5.3 (Zhipu AI, 2026). We pair these models with four harnesses: Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025), Codex (OpenAI, 2025), nanobot (HKUDS, 2025), and minimal tool-call loop. We evaluate Claude Code and Codex with their own models, while nanobot provides common harness across all six models to disentangle model and harness effects. The end-to-end study (Section 4.5) additionally uses Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic, 2026a) with Claude Code. Appendix C.3 contains full model and harness configurations.

sections.title: 4.1 AGENTS FIND SUBSTANTIAL SPEEDUPS
sections.content: Strong coding agents can exploit substantial optimization headroom in production kernels. On SVE, the best systems reach 2.74 the ncnn reference, 1.95 the llama.cpp reference, and 1.56 the SIMD Loops reference  (Table 2)  . In contrast, compiler-based automatic optimization remains far behind expert references, with even -O3 and SVE reaching at most 0.47. The -O3, SVE-enabled build is also the code that each agent starts from. Every system is faster than this -O3 reference across all four repositories (2.419.8; Appendix D). Highly tuned vendor kernels remain substantially more competitive. On the six KleidiAI kernels with SVE expert references, no evaluated system matches the vendor implementations in geometric mean; the best, Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8, reaches 0.70, beating the reference on two kernels but falling behind on the other four. Agents exploit headroom in general-purpose production libraries, but matching specialized vendor kernels is harder.

sections.title: 4.2 ADAPTING TO EVOLVING HARDWARE
sections.content: Agents struggle more with the programming-model shift to SME2. The biggest drop appears on SME2, which introduces streaming mode and ZA matrix tiles instead of just adding more vector instructions. On the same KleidiAI kernels, performance relative to the expert reference falls from SVE to SME2 for three of the five models: the SME2-to-SVE ratios are 0.42, 0.46, and 0.41 for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GLM-5.3, and GPT-5.6-luna, while the performance of the Claude models remains similar  (Table 4)  . GLM-5.3, the strongest of the five models on SVE, falls to less than half, so doing well on SVE does not carry over when new extension requires different programming style. We also run the fixed-machine ladder on Apple M4, with GPT-5.6-luna as the base model and nanobot as harness. Over three seeds, exposing streaming SVE lowers Speedup@40 from 0.141 (Neon only) to 0.059, and exposing full SME2 recovers part of the loss, to 0.085  (Table 3)  . Neon > SME2 > streaming SVE holds in every seed. The performance gap mostly comes from the different optimization paths that the agent applied. With streaming SVE available, the agent almost abandons Neon and settles on streaming SVE or falls back to plain if compilation or correctness errors repeatedly happen. With full SME2 available, the recovery over streaming SVE does not come from ZA outer products: the agent simply keeps Neon kernel more often than with streaming SVE only (Appendix G). None of the final SME2-tier kernels use ZA outer products, and across all SME2 runs the agent writes ZA code only twice, with neither version passing. Streaming and ZA code also fail to compile more often: in the first seed, 13% of compiles fail on the Neon tier, 20% with streaming SVE and 24% with full SME2 (Appendix G). SME2 Case Study. On gemm_bf16_n512_k512, Claude Opus 4.8 switches to streaming mode and uses MOPA/ZA accumulation, reaching 0.94 the expert implementation. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, in contrast, stay with older vector-style implementations and reach only 0.06 and 0.05. The same holds across kernels: nearly all final SVE solutions use SVE intrinsics, but of the 18 final SME2 solutions on the six KleidiAI kernels of Table 4 (three seeds), only 15 (Opus), 5 (Sonnet), 5 (GLM-5.3), and 1 (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) use the ZA tiles (Appendix F). Appendix E.2 traces in detail representative SME2 optimization trajectory. Agents adapt more readily to incremental ISA extensions. By contrast, the move from SVE to SVE2 costs much less. On the eight SIMD Loops kernels whose expert SVE2 implementation needs SVE2-only instructions, the SVE2-to-SVE ratios are between 0.94 and 1.05 for every model  (Table 4)  , and most final SVE2 solutions of the Claude models use the experts SVE2-only instructions (Appendix F). The fixed-machine instruction ladder on Graviton4 shows the same pattern: Neon and SVE2 reach 1.105 and 1.101  (Table 3)  . sections.title: 4.3 AGENT GAINS DEPEND ON EXPERT HEADROOM
sections.content: Across the 79 SVE kernels, median agent Speedup@40 decreases as the expert reference becomes stronger relative to unvectorized scalar code (Spearman ρ = 0.69; ρ = 0.75 within llama.cpp; Figure 3). Thus, large Speedup@40 values often reflect under-optimized reference paths rather than unusually strong agent performance. This is clear in llama.cpp RMSNorm: the reference is only 1.3 faster than scalar, while agents beat it by median 6.0. Conversely, for q4_K_M GEMM and MoE, the expert implementations are already 2529 faster than scalar, and agents reach only 0.570.69 of the expert.

sections.title: 4.4 WHAT IMPROVES AGENT OPTIMIZATION?
sections.content: As shown in Figure 4, most of the improvement is realized within the first 40 tool calls, but budget beyond 40 still pays off: Claude Sonnet 4.6 is 2325% higher at 100 calls than at 40. This additional gain, however, comes mainly from few kernels undergoing structural rewrites between roughly 40 and 60 calls, and past 60 calls the curves are largely converged. Arm documentation does not improve performance on SVE. On SME2 it raises Speedup@40 (0.130 vs. 0.083), but not through better SME2 code: with the documentation, no best version uses streaming SVE (vs. 6 without it), 14 of the 20 use Neon (vs. 7), and compile errors drop from 102 to 54. Putting common SME2 pitfalls in the prompt, with failure examples, doubles Speedup@40 on the 20 KleidiAI SME2 kernels (0.083 to 0.167), but 5 of the 20 kernels get worse. All 18 kernels use Graviton4s i8mm instructions together with shape-specific tiling, layout, and prefetching. Individual kernels average 1.5 faster than llama.cpps own repacked kernels if measured in isolation. Unlike llama.cpps general kernels, the agent-generated kernels are specialized to the target models shapes, so this shows the potential of automatic deployment-time specialization over expert libraries. Appendix E.1 provides complete setup and detailed results.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Kernel optimization across hardware. Recent work evaluates whether language models and coding agents can generate efficient kernels for given hardware target or programming interface. KernelBench and TritonBench study GPU kernel generation (Ouyang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), while MobileKernelBench and SimdBench extend to mobile CPUs and SIMD intrinsics (Zou et al., 2026; He et al., 2025). Other benchmarks extend kernel evaluation across architectures and devices (Li et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2025; Zang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025). These works primarily evaluate performance on fixed target or set of hardware targets. In contrast, KERNELSHIFT organizes hardware as sequence of successive architectural extensions and evaluates matched kernel tasks across generations where coverage permits. This lets us study adaptation to new instructions and programming abstractions. Coding agents for performance optimization. Recent coding agents improve programs through iterative execution and feedback (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). For kernel optimization, GPU Kernel Scientist and CudaForge use iterative search and hardware feedback, while AdaExplore combines execution-driven adaptation with diversity-preserving search (Andrews & Witteveen, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Du et al., 2026). More recent systems train kernel-optimization agents with reinforcement learning (Dai et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026). These works show rapid progress in agentic kernel optimization. KERNELSHIFT provides both controlled benchmark and hardware-in-theloop environment for testing whether such agents can adapt their optimization strategies as hardware evolves. Automated program optimization. broader line of work studies program optimization using learned cost models, reinforcement learning, and search (Chen et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2020; Trofin et al., 2021; Cummins et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2025; Mankowitz et al., 2023; Fawzi et al., 2022; Novikov et al., 2025). However, automated optimizers can still fall short of expert implementations when performance depends on hardware-specific transformations (Mendis et al., 2019; Tschand

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced KERNELSHIFT, benchmarking pipeline and set of environments to study how well coding agents optimize kernels as hardware evolves. Our results show that stronger agents can match or beat production kernels on established vector ISAs, but they struggle with programming-model shifts such as SME2. At the same time, the end-to-end speedups that agent-written kernels deliver on two LLMs highlight the potential of agent-driven kernel optimization in real deployments. Limitations. Newer hardware is harder to evaluate because strong expert implementations are often not available, which limits how many kernels we can compare across generations; in particular, our SME2 evidence rests on the 20 KleidiAI kernels that have an SME2 expert reference. Our experiments also focus on Arm CPUs, so it remains to be seen whether the same trends hold for other architectures such as x86 or GPUs. Finally, our kernel-level evaluation is single-core and does not cover all effects that may appear in multi-core deployment.

sections.title: B TASK CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: B.1 CONSTRUCTION SKILLS AND VALIDATION SCRIPTS Task construction is carried out by coding agent that follows written procedures, which we call construction skills. Each skill is document that the agent loads on demand. It states what to extract from the request and the given resources, the artifact to produce and its schema, the checks to run afterwards, and list of known failure modes. Each skill calls deterministic scripts for the mechanical steps, such as capturing workload shapes and building and running task. The agent supplies the judgment these scripts cannot, such as which dimensions are fixed per kernel, how to call the source library, and which workloads fill coverage gap, and it runs the validation on the target machine. For the entire generation pipeline, we use Claude Code with sonnet-5 as the base model. gen-definition writes Four skills cover the benchmarking pipeline of Section 2.1. the kernel specification (Figure 5), gen-workload collects its workloads (Figure 6), gen-candidate-solution renders the scalar starting implementation (Figure 7), and gen-baseline-solution wraps the source librarys kernel as the expert reference (Figure 8).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Construction Skill: gen-definition Task Description Design and write Definition JSON for new operator. This skill writes the structural schema only; concrete tensor sizes are added afterwards by gen-workload. The reference function inside the definition is correctness oracle, not workload. What to Extract from the Request * Op name and what it computes (enough to write reference function) * Axes: which are fixed per kernel configuration (const) and which vary per workload (var) * Input and output tensors: names, shapes (as lists of axis names), and dtypes * Constraints expressing derived output axes in terms of other axes * reference implementation in NumPy or PyTorch If the request is underspecified in any of these areas, ask before generating. Workflow 0. If the op comes from real model, extract its shapes from the Hugging Face config.json or from torchvision forward hooks (no weights are downloaded), and record the source as model:<name> tag. 1. Read one or two existing definitions of the closest operator family. 2. Elicit the design from the user until it is unambiguous, including which framework supplies the expert reference (baseline-solution:<framework> tag). Always ask; do not infer it from the model or the dtype. 3. Present the complete definition and its output path. Wait for explicit confirmation before writing. 4. The agent enables these instructions per function and combines them with shape-specific tiling, layout, and prefetching. sections.title: H CONTAMINATION STATEMENT
sections.content: Because ncnn, llama.cpp, SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI are public, expert code may exist in models training data. However, on most ncnn, llama.cpp, and SIMD Loops kernels, agents exceed the expert code rather than reproducing it, and use intrinsics not in library code and different algorithm structures. Further, the task setup does not match the library: agents start from portable scalar code with benchmark-specific interfaces. Finally, KleidiAIs SME2 expert kernels are also public, yet agents fall far short of them. As direct test, on the 20 KleidiAI SME2 kernels of Table 3 (full SME2 arm), the 6 whose expert micro-kernels were added to KleidiAI after the knowledge cutoff of GPT-5.6-luna (2026-02-16) score about the same as the 14 older ones (geometric-mean Speedup@40 0.088 vs. 0.082). The workloads used for the correctness check and for timing are also hidden from the agents.
